title: Desertification, UNCCD and Land Degradation Neutrality

cards.h: Land is a climate and food issue
cards.b:
Soil loss and desert spread threaten farm output and rural jobs. Prelims asks about UNCCD, Land Degradation Neutrality (LDN) and the India hosting of COP14. Mains asks about causes and solutions.

This lesson focuses on the global treaty and India's numbers.

A common trap is to treat desertification as the growth of existing deserts. It is a degradation process in dry lands.

Land degradation is the loss of land's productivity. Desertification is degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas caused by climate and human activity. It does not mean desert sand dunes spreading only. Causes: overgrazing, deforestation, bad irrigation (salinity and waterlogging), shifting cultivation, mining and climate change.

Soil erosion by water is the biggest single process in India, followed by wind erosion and salinity.

The UN Convention to Combat Desertification was adopted in Paris in 1994 and came into force in 1996. It is one of the three Rio Conventions with the CBD and UNFCCC. Its Secretariat is in Bonn. India ratified it in 1996. The convention stresses a bottom-up approach and national action programmes.

At Rio+20, the world agreed to aim for a land-degradation-neutral world. SDG 15.3 targets Land Degradation Neutrality (LDN) by 2030: loss of healthy land balanced by restoration.

India hosted UNCCD COP14 at Greater Noida in September 2019, with the theme "Restore land, sustain future". The Delhi Declaration came out of it. India raised its restoration pledge from 21 to 26 million hectares by 2030. India held the COP presidency until COP15 (Abidjan, 2022) and has the Centre of Excellence at the Indian Council of Forestry Research and Education (ICFRE) in Dehradun for LDN. The 2019 COP also launched a Peace Forest Initiative.

The Desertification and Land Degradation Atlas (ISRO's Space Applications Centre, 2021, for 2018-19) said about 97.85 million hectares, about 29.7 percent of India's land, is degraded. The most affected states include Rajasthan, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Jharkhand, Odisha, Madhya Pradesh and Ladakh. Water erosion is the leading process, followed by vegetation degradation and wind erosion.

The Thar Desert, the Rann of Kutch and the cold desert of Ladakh are key arid zones.

• Afforestation and shelterbelts; the Aravalli Green Wall idea mirrors the African Great Green Wall (Sahel).
  • Soil conservation: contour bunding, terracing, check dams, and no-till farming.
  • Watershed programmes: Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana (watershed development), earlier IWMP.
  • Soil Health Card scheme (2015).
  • Green India Mission, MGNREGA works on land and water.
  • Agroforestry and rotational grazing.

Ravine reclamation in Chambal and sand-dune stabilisation in Rajasthan are classic examples. The Indira Gandhi Canal greened parts of the Thar but caused waterlogging in places.

Some drylands are native open grasslands, and tree planting there harms them. The "wasteland" label invites diversion for solar parks and mines. Critics say restoration should focus on natural ecosystems, not just tree cover. Another dispute is whether farm subsidies for water and fertiliser drive salinity.

LDN is linked to the Bonn Challenge, the Green India Mission and NDC targets (a carbon sink of 2.5 to 3 billion tonnes by 2030). The Central Arid Zone Research Institute (CAZRI) at Jodhpur studies arid lands. Efforts like soil carbon, natural farming and Mission LiFE link land to climate.

• UNCCD: 1994 Paris; in force 1996; Bonn.
  • COP14: Greater Noida, 2019.
  • Pledge: 26 million ha by 2030.
  • SDG 15.3: LDN.
  • Degraded land: about 29.7 percent (2018-19).

Also remember that UNCCD is one of the three Rio Conventions, with the CBD and UNFCCC, and that its Secretariat sits in Bonn.

Prelims-style: "Where was UNCCD COP14 held?" (Greater Noida). "Which Rio Convention addresses desertification?" (UNCCD).

Mains-style: "What is Land Degradation Neutrality? Examine India's progress." Structure: define; scale (97.85 million ha); causes; UNCCD and COP14; Indian programmes; challenges; way forward.

Use the 97.85 million hectare figure and the 26 million hectare pledge together in a conclusion.
